Analysis by Richard Cowan 

Late last month, the LA media carried a story about “marijuana vending machines” and the phone started ringing at the NORML office. Everyone everywhere in the media wanted a “fair and balanced” comment on this hilarious new development in the hilarious world of marijuana where everything is just one joke after another. 

See

and 

The Murder of Robin Prosser. An Indictment of Karen Tandy and Motorola – By Their Own Words and Standards. 

However, last Friday another story about the vending machines hit the wires, and media interest disappeared. The Associated Press reported, “UN board says marijuana machines illegal 

Marijuana vending machines in Los Angeles violate international treaties and should be shut down, the U.N.-affiliated drug control board said Friday. 

‘The International Narcotics Control Board is deeply concerned about reports that computerized vending machines to dispense cannabis (marijuana) have been put into operation in Los Angeles,’ Philip O. Emafo, president of the board, said in a statement.” 

Think about this for a moment. 

The vending machines do not do anything new. Medical marijuana has been sold in California for years. The machines are for patients and are not accessible to the general public. 

On the other hand, think about the importance of the UN telling the US how to enforce its laws. Imagine for a moment that the UN said that the US has to ban guns, for example. 

Blue helmets! Black helicopters! Get the UN Out Of the US!!! 

Or consider that in her debate with Barack Obama, Hillary Clinton claimed that she voted against a law that would have inhibited President Bush’s ability to start the Iraq war, because it would have subordinated the US to the UN. (That was really not an accurate description of the bill, but that is irrelevant here.) The point is simply that even a “liberal Democrat” like Hillary Clinton would object to subordinating the US to the UN. That is a serious issue.

Unless it involves marijuana, and nothing involving marijuana is ever serious. So for your continued amusement, let us look at what the UN narks have to say. 

UNIS/NAR/1023 8 February 2008 

Marijuana Vending Machines in Los Angeles are Contrary to International Drug Control Treaties, says INCB 

VIENNA, 8 February (UN Information Service) -- "The International Narcotics Control Board (INCB) is deeply concerned about reports that computerized vending machines to dispense cannabis (marijuana) have been put into operation in Los Angeles," said Dr. Philip O. Emafo, President of the Board. The Board concludes its 91st session today in Vienna. "We know that the use of cannabis is illegal under federal law of the United States and we trust the authorities will stop such activities, which contravene the international drug control treaties," he added. 

California is one of 11 states of the United States of America which allows medical use of cannabis, though such use continues to be illegal under federal law. In June 2005, the US Supreme Court confirmed the right of the Government to enforce the prohibition on the use of cannabis in a state that removed state-level criminal penalties on the use, possession and cultivation of cannabis for medical purposes. 

See 

Program Notes for the MarijuanaNews World Report June 6, 2005 Supreme Court: 6 To 3 Against Patients’ Right To Grow. Rehnquist, Thomas Dissent Political Victory. State Laws Unaffected. 

Cannabis is included in Schedules I and IV of the Single Convention on Narcotic Drugs of 1961, as amended by the 1972 Protocol (1961 Convention). Substances in Schedule IV are those considered particularly liable to abuse. 

For some years there have been various claims about the therapeutic usefulness of cannabis or cannabis extracts. Scientific research concerning this question is in progress in several countries. So far, the results of research regarding the potential therapeutic usefulness have been limited. 

(MarijuanaNews note: Such intellectual dishonesty is typical of the UN narks. There are vast amounts of research and clinical data demonstrating the medical utility and safety of cannabis, including the 1999 Institute of Medicine Report, which flatly stated, “"There is no clear alternative for people suffering from chronic conditions 

that might be relieved by smoking marijuana, such as pain or AIDS wasting.")

INCB has confirmed in its annual reports that it welcomes sound scientific research on the therapeutic usefulness of cannabis. The Board requested governments concerned to share the results of such research, when available, with the Board, the World Health Organization (WHO) and the international community. 

The Board has repeatedly expressed its concern that, without having reported conclusive research results to WHO, the Governments of Canada and the Netherlands authorized the use of cannabis for medical purposes. 

(MarijuanaNews note: The UN treaties all have provisions making them subject to the signatories own constitutions, which is a rather large loophole, and this statement ignores the fact that Canada was ordered by its courts to provide a workable system to provide medical cannabis to patients. Consequently, Canada is not in violation of its treaty obligations. The same is basically true of the Dutch.)

and

The Board is also concerned that cannabis is used for medical purposes in some jurisdictions of the United States without having definitive proof of its efficacy. 

The control measures applied in California for the cultivation, production and use of cannabis do not meet the control standards set in the 1961 Convention to prevent diversion of narcotic drugs for illicit use. Such standards require, inter alia, the control of cultivation and production of cannabis by a national cannabis agency, and detailed record keeping and reporting on the activities with cannabis, including reporting to INCB. 

The International Narcotics Control Board (INCB) is an independent control organ, established by the Single Convention on Narcotic Drugs of 1961, as amended by the 1972 Protocol, for monitoring the implementation of the international drug control treaties by Governments and for providing assistance to Governments in this regard.
